questions.question_text: Which of the following expressions is identically equal to $\sin(-\theta) + \cos(-\theta)$?

options.why: Treated sine as an even function; $\sin(-\theta)=-\sin\theta$, so the sine term must be negated.
Treated cosine as an odd function; $\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta$, so the cosine term is not negated.
Reversed the parity of both functions, treating sine as even and cosine as odd.

questions.question_text: Which of the following expressions is identically equal to $\tan(-\theta)$?

options.why: Treated tangent as an even function; $\tan$ is odd, so $\tan(-\theta)=-\tan\theta$.
Confused the negative-angle identity with the reciprocal identity.
Both inverted and negated the ratio instead of only negating $\tan\theta$.

questions.solution_text: $\tan(-\theta)=-\tan\theta$ because tangent is an odd function.

questions.question_text: If $\tan(-x) = 2.5$, what is the value of $\tan x$?

options.why: Ignored the negative sign; $\tan(-x)=-\tan x=2.5$, so $\tan x=-2.5$.
Inverted the ratio instead of negating it; negative-angle relationships negate the value.
Both inverted and negated the ratio; only a sign change applies: $\tan x=-\tan(-x)$.

questions.question_text: If $\sin x = -0.7$, what is the value of $\sin(-x)$?

options.why: Failed to apply the sign change; $\sin(-x)=-\sin x=-(-0.7)=0.7$.
Subtracted from $1$ instead of applying the negative-angle identity $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$.
Subtracted from $1$ and made negative rather than evaluating $-(-0.7)=0.7$.
Treated $\cos(-\theta)$ as $-\cos\theta$; cosine is even, so $\cos(-\theta)+\cos\theta=\cos\theta+\cos\theta=2\cos\theta$.
Confused with the Pythagorean identity $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$.
Added the interior angles instead of combining the outside trigonometric terms.
Missed that the product of two negatives is positive: $(-\sin\theta)(-\tan\theta)=\sin\theta\tan\theta$.
Replaced tangent with sine without dividing by cosine, and introduced an incorrect negative sign.
Replaced tangent with sine instead of keeping $\tan\theta$.

questions.question_text: On the unit circle, the terminal point for angle $\theta$ is $(x,y)$. What is the terminal point for angle $-\theta$, and what does this establish?

options.why: Reflected across the $y$-axis instead of the $x$-axis; clockwise rotation reflects across the $x$-axis.

options.text: $(-x,-y)$, establishing that both sine and cosine are negated
options.why: Reflected through the origin (rotation by $180^{\circ}$) rather than reflecting across the $x$-axis.
Reflected across the line $y=x$ (the inverse function reflection) instead of the $x$-axis.

questions.solution_text:
Rotating by $-\theta$ reflects the terminal arm across the $x$-axis, giving coordinates $(x,-y)$.
Therefore $\cos(-\theta)=x=\cos\theta$ and $\sin(-\theta)=-y=-\sin\theta$.

questions.question_text: Determine whether the function $f(x) = x\cos(-x)$ is odd, even, or neither, with algebraic justification.

options.text: Even function, because $\cos(-x) = \cos x$ so $f(-x) = f(x)$
options.why: Ignored the factor of $-x$ from substituting into the outer $x$, which negates the expression.

options.text: Even function, because $(-x)(-\cos x) = x\cos x = f(x)$
options.why: Incorrectly treated cosine as an odd function, writing $\cos(-x)=-\cos x$.

options.text: Neither odd nor even, because $f(-x) = -x\cos(-x)$ cannot be simplified to $\pm f(x)$
options.why: Failed to apply the negative-angle identity $\cos(-x)=\cos x$ to simplify $f(-x)$.

questions.solution_text:
$f(x) = x\cos(-x) = x\cos x$
$f(-x) = (-x)\cos(-(-x)) = -x\cos x = -f(x)$
Since $f(-x) = -f(x)$, $f(x)$ is an odd function.

questions.question_text: Determine whether the function $g(x) = x^3\sin(-x) + \cos(-x)$ is odd, even, or neither, with algebraic justification.

options.text: Even function, because $g(-x) = -x^3\sin x + \cos x = g(x)$
Odd function, because $g(-x) = x^3\sin x - \cos x = -g(x)$
options.why: Incorrectly simplified $(-x)^3\sin(x)$ to $x^3\sin x$ and negated $\cos x$.

options.text: Neither odd nor even, because $g(x)$ is the sum of an odd term and an even term
options.why: Overlooked that $x^3\sin(-x)=-x^3\sin x$ is a product of two odd components, making it an even term.
Swapped the parities of sine and cosine, treating sine as even and cosine as odd.

questions.solution_text:
$g(x) = x^3(-\sin x) + \cos x = -x^3\sin x + \cos x$
$g(-x) = (-x)^3\sin(-(-x)) + \cos(-(-x)) = -x^3\sin x + \cos x = g(x)$
Since $g(-x) = g(x)$, $g(x)$ is an even function.
